items.title: 35日でフロントエンドの基礎を完全に理解する #16 - CSSレイアウト基礎（Flexbox・Grid・レスポンシブ）
items.summary: この記事で学ぶこと #15 では、型を持ったAPIクライアントでバックエンドとデータをやり取りする設計を学びました。今回はいったん通信の話を離れ、画面の中で要素をどう並べるかという見た目の基礎に戻ります。テーマは3つです。 Flexbox で要素を1次元（横一列や縦一列）に並べる Grid で要素を2次元（行と列の格子）に並べる メディアクエリで画面の幅に応じてレイアウトを切り替える 迷ったら🔴だけ確実に（🔴 覚える、🟡 理屈、⚪ 流す）。 ! 今回はブラウザだけで試せます。#6 で作った Vue のプロジェクトは使わず、HTMLファイルを1つ作って開くだけで確認できます。 ...
items.titleJa: 35日でフロントエンドの基礎を完全に理解する #16 - CSSレイアウト基礎（Flexbox・Grid・レスポンシブ）
items.summaryJa:
本文の内容をもとに、日本語で2〜3文・約150〜200字の要約を作成します。

Flexboxは1次元の並べ方（横一列・縦一列）を扱い、主軸と交差軸の配置をjustify-contentとalign-itemsで制御する。Gridは2次元の格子配置で、grid-template-columns/rowsとgapでマス目を決め、要素は通常左上から順に配置される。レスポシブはメディアクエリで画面幅に応じて切り替え、モバイルファーストの考え方を採るのが実務的とされ、3列カードを小さな画面で1列へ切り替える例などが解説されている。

items.titleJa: コーダーからフロントエンドエンジニアへ #1-61｜オブジェクトとは何か──名前をつけて値をまとめる
items.summaryJa: オブジェクトは、キーと値の組み合わせ（プロパティ）を名前でまとめたものである。波カッコで定義し、キーと値はコロンで結び、要素はカンマで区切る。読み取りはオブジェクト名.キーとし、存在しないキーは undefined になる。値には文字列・数値・真偽値・null・配列・オブジェクト・関数など何でも入る。配列は番号で、オブジェクトは名前で区別する点が重要で、typeof は両方とも "object" を返すため、配列とオブジェクトの判定には Array.isArray を使う。さらに、オブジェクト配列の各要素は「商品オブジェクト1件」として、p.name などの形で読み取り、map などと合わせて読みやすさが向上する。

items.title: Making every harness durable
items.summary: Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike. Running harnesses in the cloud Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products. These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt. In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work. Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox. Making every harness durable We built eve and fx to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing durable-harness , which extends that durability to any harness, including Pi , OpenCode , Codex , and Claude Code . It uses the same machinery that powers Workflow SDK to survive crashes and function timeouts. With durable-harness , you can: Run any of these harnesses durably on Vercel Self-host a harness with your own Postgres instance Make your local harness workflow durable Build your own durable harness Sessions that survive a crash mid-turn Take the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back. What happens if its function times out while CI is still running? Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated. Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily. With durable-harness , a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log. Logs and queues durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a World , the Workflow SDK’s durable backend. It writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off. After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started: Completed calls never run again because their results are read from the log, so you’re never billed twice for a finished model call’s tokens. Models remember their previous calls rather than repeating them. Interrupted tools marked replay: 'safe' run again. Any other tool comes back to the model as possibly run, and the model decides whether to check. Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it. Pick your harness fx and eve are durable on their own. For the rest, durable-harness adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness. For the full setup guide for each harness, check the docs . Runs everywhere Durable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching. Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a World . durable-harness writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code: On Vercel, it uses the Vercel World . In development, it uses files on your machine . On your own servers, it uses Postgres , MongoDB, Redis, or Turso. Two variables move every agent using durable-harness to Postgres. For more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent: Check the self-hosting docs for more details. See every session in Agent Runs Agent Runs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up. Tools An agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A 'safe' tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A 'never' tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again. Here’s how the coding agent from the demo above might define its tools: A tool that reads a file or checks CI status is marked as 'safe' so it can run again automatically. A tool that posts a PR comment is marked as 'never' so that comments aren't posted twice. The following example defines a tool for each policy using the example of an agent processing a refund: For each harness’s built-in tools, like its shell and file editing, read on. Files When a harness needs a shell and files, it’s not safe to run them directly on a shared serverless function host. Many sessions can share the same function, and its filesystem isn’t guaranteed to persist between invocations. To address this, durable-harness gives you a few options: virtual() keeps the files in the session’s log, with a bash-compatible shell that can’t reach your function’s files or the network. It suits short tasks and small workspaces without starting an entire sandbox. virtual({ durable: false }) keeps the files in memory for scratch work and clears them at the end of every turn. sandbox() gives the session its own Vercel Sandbox , with /workspace on a Drive that outlives every sandbox and every function. It suits real projects and long-running work. Compare the three side by side in the docs . Each harness’s built-in tools run on the workspace you choose. With Pi, CodingTools installs Pi’s own read , write , edit , and bash , and virtualEnv() or sandboxEnv() gives them a workspace: For OpenCode, pass the workspace as workspace , and for fx, pass it to fxTools() . Claude Code and Codex always run in a Vercel Sandbox, since they expect a real shell and filesystem, and aren’t safe for multi-tenant use. Their built-in tools work on the session’s Drive once you turn them on with builtins: true . Each harness guide lists its built-in tools. Documents Some state belongs with the session but isn’t part of the conversation, such as a to-do list, a plan, or a form the agent fills in. A document is typed JSON that lives in the session’s log, so it survives a crash and moves with the session. Tools can edit documents through io.docs , and each edit commits to the log alongside the tool’s result, so the document’s durable state stays consistent with the tool calls themselves: Your app can read and edit the same document without a database of its own, and the chat route can even stream every change to your UI: In fact, the virtual() workspace from earlier is built on documents: its file tree is a document in the session’s log, and each tool call’s changes commit with its result. Learn more about tools, files, and documents and how to keep your agent secure . Wrapping up Developers choose a harness for the choices it makes about prompts, tools, and context. How it survives a crash shouldn’t be one of them. With durable-harness , a turn that loses its function partway through continues from the log on a new one, without a manual retry and without repeating what already finished. Self-hosting and portability work out of the box by building on top of the Workflow SDK’s World interface. durable-harness is open source on GitHub . Read more

items.title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
items.summary: AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn. Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache . Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter. Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway , or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions. Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions. Read more
